channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: UK GDP rose 0.7% in the third quarter, up from 0.5% in the second, with construction output contracting 0.7% (period not stated) and the ONS citing higher petrol, diesel and gas costs as a restraint, MarketScreener and the Guardian report.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that UK gross domestic product rose 0.7% in the three months to September, up from 0.5% in the second quarter and in line with the FXStreet-cited consensus forecast of 0.7%, and 1.9% on an annual basis, up from 1.4%. Growth was driven by services, which expanded 0.9%, particularly business-facing services, while production output edged up 0.1% and construction output contracted 0.7%. Monthly GDP rose 0.2% in September, against an expected flat reading, after a flat August that was revised down from 0.1%. The Guardian reports that the Office for National Statistics (ONS) cited a rise in the cost of petrol, diesel and natural gas after the re-escalation of the Middle East conflict as a factor restricting growth, and Business Day reports that the ONS cited investment in artificial intelligence as a contributing factor and describes the quarter as the strongest calendar-quarter expansion since the first quarter of 2024. The rows do not say what period the construction and production figures compare with, give construction sub-sectors or the weights of the sectors in GDP.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report national output figures with sector growth rates and the statistics office's stated drivers. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, services-led growth with falling construction output means building activity is not benefiting from the overall expansion, and higher fuel and gas costs add to costs for energy-intensive industries. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, a fall in UK construction output points to softer demand for construction materials; the rows give no figures for housebuilding, materials or manufacturing. Points that may be worth considering include the next monthly GDP release, construction output data and energy price developments.

MarketScreener | The Guardian | Business Day

item.title: The Bundesbank warns that financial stability risks have risen, calling commercial real estate vulnerabilities "pronounced", with price declines possible on rate rises and potential selling pressure from the real estate fund sector, Handelsblatt reports.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that the Bundesbank has warned of increased risks to financial stability, citing rising credit risks, high valuations in financial markets, risks in real estate financing, high government debt and the growing importance of private credit, that is loans from shadow banks. In several areas the Bundesbank assesses the dangers as higher than in the previous year. A focus of the report is commercial real estate, where vulnerabilities remain "pronounced" and price declines could occur because of possible interest rate rises and potential "selling pressure from the real estate fund sector". Risks have risen particularly in funds: since mid-2023 funds have increasingly flowed out of German open-ended real estate funds, and individual funds have had to suspend or restrict the redemption of shares. The row does not give the size of the outflows, loan volumes or valuations, the expected price fall, or any effect on residential real estate or construction.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a central bank's risk assessment for real estate finance, not property prices or construction activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, weaker commercial property values and fund outflows tighten financing for new projects and refurbishments. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, commercial and mixed-use construction and refurbishment in Germany depend on financing conditions, so tighter credit could slow project starts; the row gives no project or credit figures. Points that may be worth considering include the figures in the full report, commercial real estate prices and the interest rate path.

Handelsblatt

item.title: The UK sanctioned Russian oil producer Slavneft, saying it is the first country to target all of Russia's ten largest oil producers, and listed vessels including five LNG carriers and five oil tankers, MarketScreener and Interfax report.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that the UK has imposed sanctions on the Russian oil producer Slavneft and a range of energy-related entities and vessels, and the UK says it has become the first country to target all of Russia's 10 largest oil producers. The measures also cover vessels carrying Russian oil and liquefied natural gas, major coal companies and Rosneft's Vostok Oil project. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the sanctions aim to turn the screws on Russia's oil revenues and drive forward an end to what he called the Kremlin's needless war. Interfax reports that the UK Foreign Office added ten vessels to its Russia sanctions list, although the row names five LNG carriers, five oil tankers and an LNG storage and transshipment unit operated by Novatek, eleven items in all, citing their alleged involvement in transporting Russian oil, petroleum products or liquefied natural gas to third countries. The rows do not give the volumes of Russian oil and gas affected, the date the measures take effect, the response of Russia or of buyers, or any parallel steps by the EU or the United States.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report sanctions listings, not changes in trade flows or prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, listing producers and ships raises the cost and difficulty of moving Russian oil and gas to buyers, with effects that depend on how much trade shifts to other channels. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, oil and gas are the feedstock and energy base of petrochemical raw materials, and tighter restrictions on Russian flows add to supply and shipping uncertainty in energy markets; the rows give no price or volume data. Points that may be worth considering include oil and gas prices, tanker rates and any further sanctions steps.

MarketScreener | Interfax

item.title: The Court of Justice of the EU rejected Poland's challenges to seven EU climate laws on 12 November, including the 2035 zero-emission car target and carbon pricing for heating and transport, ruling that a qualified majority was enough, Politico reports.
item.description:
Politico reports that on 12 November 2026 the Court of Justice of the EU rejected challenges to seven major EU climate laws, including the 2035 target for zero-emission cars and carbon pricing for heating and transport. The rulings uphold key parts of the Green Deal and close a legal campaign launched by Poland's previous nationalist Law and Justice government. Poland argued that the laws would fundamentally reshape its coal-dependent energy system and therefore needed unanimous approval by EU governments, effectively giving Poland a veto. The court ruled that the measures could be adopted by a qualified majority of member countries. The row does not name the other five laws, give the dates from which the car target and the heating and transport carbon price apply, say whether the current Polish government supports the laws, or mention any appeal or any change to the laws under discussion.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a court ruling on the legal basis of laws, not a change in their content. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the ruling removes a legal uncertainty over laws that set a vehicle target and a carbon price on heating and transport fuels, which carmakers, building owners and energy users take into their planning. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the car target bears on the materials used in electric vehicles and the heating and transport carbon price on the economics of building renovation and on logistics costs; the row gives no cost or volume figures. Points that may be worth considering include the start dates of the carbon pricing and any proposals to revise the car target.

Politico

item.title: Spain's construction sector had an average of 1,518,556 affiliated workers in October, up 1.5% from September and 7.3% from a year earlier, the best October since 2010, a construction observatory barometer shows.
item.description:
The Barometer of the Construction Industry Observatory, reported by the Fundación Laboral de la Construcción, shows an average of 1,518,556 affiliated workers in the sector in October 2026, 1.5% more than in September and 7.3%, or 103,405 people, more than in October 2025, the best October since 2010. The General Regime accounts for 1,094,354 of them, 1.7% more than in September and 42,883, or 4.1%, more than a year earlier. By activity, civil engineering grew most (27.8%), followed by specialised construction activities (12.9%), while building construction fell 11.9% (the row does not state the comparison period for these rates), which the row says is largely explained by the application of the new national classification of economic activities (CNAE-2025). The row does not give output, orders, permits or housing starts, the split between residential and non-residential work, the reasons for the growth or how much of the shift between activity categories is due to reclassification.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports employment in the sector, not construction output or orders. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, employment growth in civil engineering and specialised trades may point to work under way, but the row says the fall in building construction is largely explained by reclassification and does not say how much of the movement in the other categories is too, so the category figures may not show a change in activity. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, specialised construction trades such as finishing and installation use bonding, sealing and coating products, and civil engineering uses sealants and coatings in infrastructure; the row gives no materials figures. Points that may be worth considering include Spanish construction output and permit data, the November affiliation figures and housing and infrastructure policy.

Fundación Laboral de la Construcción

item.title: Brazil registered 2.41 million cars and light commercial vehicles in January to October, up 17.3% on a year earlier, while Argentine plants shipped 144,709 vehicles to Brazil, down 8.4%, La Nación reports.
item.description:
La Nación reports that Brazil registered 2.41 million automobiles and light commercial vehicles between January and October, 17.3% more than a year earlier. In the same period Argentine plants sent 144,709 vehicles to Brazil, 8.4% fewer, a fall the paper puts at around 13,250 units that stopped crossing into the main market of Argentina's industry. The row does not state the comparison period for the 8.4% fall, name the data source for the Brazilian registrations, give the split by fuel type or brand, the share of imports, the monthly trend or the reasons for the rise, or Argentina's total output.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports registrations and shipments from Argentine plants to Brazil. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rise of this size in Brazil's new vehicle market can support local assembly and component demand, while a fall in Argentine shipments to its main market suggests, although shipments and registrations are different measures, that the extra Brazilian demand did not go to Argentine plants. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly in Brazil and Argentina uses bonding, sealing and coating materials, so the origin of the vehicles sold in Brazil bears on where that demand arises; the row gives no origin split for the rest of the market. Points that may be worth considering include the November registrations and the origin of vehicles sold in Brazil.

La Nación

item.title: BMW cut shifts in Regensburg, Leipzig and Oxford and Skoda's Enyaq and Elroq output suffered for weeks from a wiring harness shortage that Handelsblatt links to Russian attacks on a supplier's Ukrainian plants, citing industry circles.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that BMW has cut shifts in Regensburg, Leipzig and Oxford because of a shortage of wiring harnesses from Ukraine, and that the Volkswagen subsidiary Skoda has had production of its Enyaq and Elroq electric models affected for weeks by the missing parts. According to Handelsblatt information from industry circles, the bottlenecks are related to Russian attacks on the Ukrainian plants of the German supplier Kromberg & Schubert near Zhytomyr and Lutsk, which have been attacked repeatedly in recent months. The row does not give the number of vehicles or shifts lost, the dates of the attacks, the share of each carmaker's harness supply that comes from these plants, alternative sourcing or restart plans, or statements by BMW, Skoda or the supplier.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports supply shortfalls at carmakers, with the link to attacks attributed to unnamed industry sources. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, wiring harnesses are labour-intensive components made in a limited number of locations, so attacks on a supplier's plants that disrupt harness output can stop assembly of the models that use them regardless of demand. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, lost vehicle output reduces consumption of bonding, sealing and coating materials in the affected assembly plants; the row gives no output or materials figures. Points that may be worth considering include the duration of the shift cuts, the supplier's production status and carmakers' alternative sourcing.

Handelsblatt

item.title: The Bundestag passed a law that, if the Bundesrat approves, eases environmental rules and deadlines for building military training areas, depots and barracks and gives Bundeswehr projects "overriding public interest", Wallstreet:online reports.
item.description:
Wallstreet:online reports that the Bundestag has passed a law on Bundeswehr infrastructure. If the Bundesrat approves it, environmental regulations for the construction of military training areas, ammunition depots and soldier accommodation will be relaxed and deadlines shortened, which the row says will simplify and speed up the construction of barracks and other military facilities. The law would also grant Bundeswehr construction projects an "overriding public interest", so that the responsible authorities give them preferential treatment. The row does not give the vote result, the date of the Bundesrat session, the budget or number of projects affected, which environmental rules are relaxed or by how much, or the expected construction volume.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a Bundestag decision on procedures that still needs Bundesrat approval, not construction orders or spending. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, shorter approval deadlines and looser environmental requirements can bring projects to construction sooner and allow more projects to proceed at once. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, barracks, depots and training facilities are non-residential buildings that use bonding, sealing and coating products, so faster approval could bring demand forward in Germany; the row gives no volumes or budgets. Points that may be worth considering include the Bundesrat vote, the defence construction budget and tender volumes.

Wallstreet:online

item.title: The Center of Automotive Management finds surveyed carmakers' operating margin fell to 3.6% from an average of 4% in the first nine months, with operating profit down 11% year on year while sales fell 1.9%, Frankfurter Rundschau reports.
item.description:
Frankfurter Rundschau reports an analysis by the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in which the operating margin of the surveyed manufacturers fell from an average of 4% to 3.6% in the first nine months. Operating profit declined by 11% from the same period last year to EUR 60.4 billion, while sales shrank by 1.9%. German manufacturers are particularly under pressure: Volkswagen reached an operating margin of only 0.03% after high special charges, down from 2.3% a year earlier, and BMW fell from 8.1% to 5.6%. Mercedes-Benz raised its group margin from 4.4% to 5.5%, primarily on better results in vans and financial services, and the row also says operating profit in the passenger car business fell by around 56%, without saying whose. The row does not name the manufacturers surveyed or give their number, margins for other groups, the size of Volkswagen's special charges, or causes beyond the Volkswagen charges and the Mercedes-Benz business mix.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports profit margins, operating profit and sales, without saying whether sales are in value or units, and not orders. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, carmakers with falling profits tend to press suppliers on prices and to defer or cancel projects. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle manufacturing is a large user of bonding, sealing and coating materials, so margin pressure at German carmakers can show up in supplier price negotiations and in the pace at which new materials are qualified; the row gives no purchasing or materials figures. Points that may be worth considering include full-year results, German carmakers' production plans and supplier cost programmes.

Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: Spain's chemical industry faced an additional EUR 1.23 billion in energy costs, EUR 640 million from natural gas prices and EUR 590 million from energy prices, after the invasion of Iran and the Hormuz closure, Cinco Días reports.
item.description:
Cinco Días reports that the chemical industry operating in Spain has been hit by a double increase in energy and gas costs, which the row ties to the "invasion of Iran" and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The row puts the additional cost at EUR 1.23 billion for these companies, EUR 640 million from the rise in natural gas prices and EUR 590 million from the rise in energy prices. Teresa Rasero, president of the Spanish Chemical Industry Business Federation (Feique), highlighted that since 2019 the price of electricity has doubled, CO2 emission rights have tripled, gas has quintupled and adjustment services have increased ninefold. The row does not give the period the EUR 1.23 billion covers, who calculated it or the baseline it is measured against, the number of companies, the sector's total energy bill, whether the costs have been passed on in selling prices, or any production cuts.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports an additional cost figure for one country's chemical industry and a federation's description of price rises since 2019, not market prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, gas and electricity are major cost items in chemical production, so higher energy costs squeeze margins and can lead producers to raise prices, reduce output or move production. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, energy-intensive raw materials and intermediates supplied from Spain and elsewhere in Europe could carry higher prices; the row gives no product prices. Points that may be worth considering include European gas and power prices, further cost estimates from the federation and chemical output data.

Cinco Días

item.title: The German Chemical Industry Association raised its 2026 sales forecast to 3.5% growth from 2.5%, with third-quarter revenue up 5.8% year on year, driven in particular by prices, while production fell 3.5% (base not stated), Süddeutsche Zeitung reports.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung reports that the German Chemical Industry Association (VCI) now expects sales in 2026 to grow 3.5% on the previous year, after forecasting 2.5% before. Third-quarter revenue rose to EUR 53 billion, 5.8% more than in the same period last year, with higher prices in particular driving the rise. Production in the quarter fell 3.5% and the number of employees fell 2.5% to around 464,000. The row does not say what the production and employment declines are measured against, give the size of the price rise behind the revenue figure, a breakdown by sub-sector, capacity utilisation, or the VCI's forecast for production, prices or the fourth quarter.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports sector revenue, production and employment, with the revenue rise attributed in particular to prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, revenue that rises while production falls can reflect higher selling prices rather than higher volumes and can point to cost pass-through more than to stronger demand, although the row does not say what the production decline is measured against. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German chemical producers supply raw materials, additives and intermediates, so price-led revenue growth can mean higher input prices for formulators, while falling production may signal soft volumes or capacity cuts; the row gives no product-level figures. Points that may be worth considering include the VCI's fourth-quarter figures, production and capacity utilisation data and raw-material price developments.

Süddeutsche Zeitung
